title: Teachers, Trust and AI: Why Abuse of Educators Is Part of a Bigger Post-Covid Crisis
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that rising verbal abuse and hostility toward teachers in England is not merely a behaviour or post-pandemic disruption problem but part of a wider societal crisis of trust in institutions and expertise, one now being accelerated by generative AI making expert judgement seem instantly replaceable. She traces how Covid placed schools at the centre of national conflict, absorbing frustration over lockdowns and lost learning at a moment when trust in government was already declining, and cites survey data on disruptive behaviour and parental hostility as symptoms of pupils and parents 'reading' teacher authority through a wider culture of suspicion. She argues AI does not create this dynamic but intensifies it: in a low-trust culture, AI becomes a weapon against professionals rather than a tool used by them. Her conclusion calls for rebuilding trust by defending teachers as professionals, not saints or service providers, alongside serious action on online abuse and careful governance of AI.
points: Hughes's central thesis links teacher abuse to a broader post-Covid crisis of trust in institutions and professional expertise, not simply to a standalone behaviour problem.
She argues AI accelerates this crisis specifically by making expert judgement feel instantly replaceable, whether via instant essay plans for pupils or AI-drafted complaints for parents.
Her framing that 'in a high-trust culture, AI is a tool used by professionals; in a low-trust culture, AI becomes a weapon against professionals' is a sharp diagnostic distinction for school leaders.
She closes by insisting rebuilding trust requires defending teachers as professionals rather than treating them as either saints or customer-service providers.
quotes: The denigration of teachers is part of a wider crisis of trust in authority, institutions and professional expertise after Covid. Now, generative AI is accelerating that crisis by making expert judgement seem instantly replaceable.
When that agreement weakens, everyday school life becomes harder. A detention becomes a personal attack. A poor grade becomes evidence of bias. A safeguarding concern becomes interference.
A pupil refusing to follow instructions is not simply failing to behave; they are rejecting the teacher's right to direct the room.
If a parent can use AI to generate a formal complaint in seconds, professional judgement becomes easier to contest. The problem is not AI itself; it is AI in a low-trust culture.
A chatbot can produce an answer. A teacher helps a young person become someone capable of judgement. In post-Covid England, this in particular, may matter more than ever.
